Introduction: The Skydiving Cat

Happy Friday, everyone! I hope you have gotten something useful out of this week as we have explored environmental nanoscience. Today, we are going to wrap up what we have been building toward by looking at the characteristics of nanomaterials that make them relevant in environmental systems. Specifically, we are going to focus on plastics.

To get us started, I want you to picture something a little unusual: a cat skydiving out of an airplane.

If we drop a cat out of a plane, what is the velocity at which that cat falls through the sky? More importantly, how many of you think that a cat falls at the same velocity as a human skydiver who has their arms stretched out and legs behind them?

It turns out, the cat actually falls slower. But why? What might slow that cat down as it falls through the fluid we call the atmosphere?

First, mass plays a role. A cat’s mass is much less than a human’s. But think about the cat itself—it has a cute little pause, it stretches out, and its fur is flapping. What does all that do? It is a lot like sticking your hand out the window of a moving car. The air pushes your hand backward against the direction you are moving. We call this force air drag. The drag of the fluid trying to pass by the creature pushes back against gravity.

As an object moves through a fluid, it will eventually reach a terminal velocity. This speed is dictated partly by mass (heavier things tend to fall faster) and partly by cross-sectional area (less area can mean falling faster, depending on the balance of forces). The terminal velocity of a cat is about 60 miles per hour, which is roughly half that of a human. If you take nothing else away from this week, you now know the terminal velocity of a cat! This is part of the reason why cats are so good at surviving falls from high places—they are excellent at slowing themselves down as they fall through the air.

Following the Plastic: Fates in the Environment

We can take this exact same concept of falling through a fluid and apply it to particles settling in water. On Wednesday, we did an exercise called “Follow the Plastic,” where we tried to predict where a released plastic particle might travel.

When we think about particles in water—whether they are pulled out into the ocean, a stream, or in runoff—we consider them to be suspended for at least part of their journey. This suspension happens because the currents and forces of the water lift and move them. But when those forces are no longer strong enough to carry the particles, they eventually settle out.

Sometimes they settle as individual particles, but often they attach to one another and grow into aggregates. These aggregates behave like larger particles, which makes them more likely to settle. For many contaminants, including toxic metals like lead or certain nanomaterials, becoming buried in the sediment is the end of the road. Once buried, they are largely removed from the environmental cycles that impact humans or ecosystems, unless something disturbs the sediment and brings them back up.

So, which properties help us predict the fate of a plastic particle?

Size is a major factor, as we just mentioned with aggregation. But what about density? We usually think of plastics as being less dense than water, meaning they should float. Yet, we find lots of plastic sinking in the environment. For a plastic particle to sink, its density must change. As plastics age and weather in the environment, their density can increase, causing them to fall out of suspension.

We usually think of plastic bottles and bags as floating on the water’s surface. Based on what we just discussed, how do these plastics eventually end up sinking to the bottom of a lake or ocean?

While many plastics start out less dense than water, their properties change over time. As they age and weather in the environment, their density can increase. They can also attach to other particles to form larger aggregates, which makes them heavy enough to overcome suspension forces and sink.

Predicting Settling Rates by Size

Let’s look at how size alone influences settling. Imagine we have three spherical particles. They all have the exact same composition and the exact same density, but they are different sizes: 12 millimeters, 5 millimeters, and 1 millimeter.

If I dropped these three particles into water, which one do you think would settle the fastest?

To test this, we can run a simple experiment using quartz pebbles (silicon dioxide). These are common natural materials, shaped into nice, rounded pebbles that approximate our three sizes. We drop them through a 30-centimeter column of water and time how long it takes them to hit the bottom.

When we run the trials, the results are quite clear. The largest particles fall through the 30 centimeters in an average of 0.64 seconds. The medium particles take about 1.0 second. The smallest particles take much longer—over two and a half seconds (2.73 seconds on average).

We see a distinct inverse relationship here: as the size of the particle decreases, the time it takes to sink through the same column of water increases.

Calculating Settling Velocity

Let’s turn those settling times into actual velocities. Velocity is simply distance divided by time. In this case, our distance is the height of the water column (0.30 meters), and our time is the average settling time we just measured.

When we plot these three points, we see that larger particles clearly have a higher velocity falling through the water. But is this a strictly linear trend? We only have three data points here, and if you look closely at the raw data from the experiment, there is some variation from one trial to the next.

What causes that variation? These are natural river pebbles, not flawless manufactured spheres. They have different textures, slight variations in exact size, and minor differences in shape. All of these characteristics affect the drag as they fall.

If we dropped three identical 5-millimeter manufactured plastic spheres instead of natural river pebbles, would we expect to see the same trial-to-trial variation in settling velocity?

We would expect much less variation. The natural pebbles have slight differences in texture, shape, and exact size, which changes the drag force acting on each individual pebble. Manufactured spheres would be much more uniform, leading to a more consistent settling velocity across trials.

This brings up an interesting question: what happens if we keep shrinking the particle? If we go smaller than one millimeter—down into the hundreds of microns, tens of microns, or all the way to the nanoscale—will the velocity just keep decreasing linearly until it hits zero?

The Forces at Play: Gravity, Buoyancy, and Drag

To answer that, we need to look at the forces acting on the particle. Let’s bring our skydiving cat back into the picture.

Just like the cat falling through the air, a particle falling through water is pulled downward by gravity. Counteracting that downward pull are buoyancy and drag.

The balance between these forces depends heavily on the particle’s properties. Diameter and density are major factors. Shape matters too—if you have ever dropped a coin into a pool, you have seen it flutter and tumble as it falls. That tumbling changes the drag constantly compared to a smooth marble dropping straight down.

The properties of the fluid also matter. Temperature changes the density of the water, and fluid motion (like currents in a river) can easily overpower the settling velocity, keeping particles suspended much longer than they would be in a still glass of water.

Shrinking Down: Stokes Settling

When we get into sizes smaller than a millimeter—down into the micron scale—the behavior of the particles changes. We enter a regime described by Stokes’ Law.

For small, approximately spherical particles in a still fluid, the settling velocity is proportional to the particle’s diameter squared.

Because of that squared relationship, if you reduce the diameter of a particle by a factor of 10, its settling velocity does not just slow down by 10 times—it slows down by a factor of 100!

Let’s test this intuition with a quick challenge.

Imagine we have three particles in the micron scale: 10 \mum, 1 \mum, and 0.1 \mum. If we assign the 10 \mum particle a relative settling speed of 1, what happens to the speed of the 1 \mum particle?

The 1 \mum particle is 10 times smaller in diameter. Because velocity scales with the square of the diameter, its speed drops by a factor of 100. So, its relative speed is 0.01.

If we shrink it by another factor of 10 down to 0.1 \mum, the speed drops by another factor of 100, giving us a relative speed of 0.0001. The velocity absolutely plummets as size goes down.

Imagine we have a 100 \mum particle and a 10 \mum particle settling in a still lake. According to Stokes’ Law, how much slower will the 10 \mum particle settle compared to the 100 \mum one?

The 10 \mum particle will settle 100 times slower than the 100 \mum particle. Because the 10 \mum particle is 10 times smaller in diameter, and Stokes settling velocity is proportional to the diameter squared, the reduction in speed is 10^2, or a factor of 100.

This is why we have to be careful. We cannot just take the macro-scale pebble data and draw a straight line all the way down to the nanoscale. The physics governing the fall shift as the scale changes.

Why This Matters for Environmental Transport

So, why do we care about these tiny differences in settling velocity?

Bigger particles settle quickly. If they are in the ocean, they hit the bottom, get buried in the sediment, and are effectively removed from environmental cycling. They might sit there for thousands of years slowly breaking down, but they aren’t interacting with the broader ecosystem.

Very small particles, however, have such a slow settling velocity that they can remain suspended for incredibly long periods, even in still water. Add a tiny bit of current, and that downward velocity is easily overcome, keeping them moving through the environment indefinitely.

And when we get down to the true nanoscale, the game changes entirely. At those tiny sizes, particles experience Brownian motion—random jittering caused by collisions with water molecules. This random displacement can completely overpower gravitational settling, meaning some nanoparticles might never settle out of solution on reasonable timescales. We will dive much deeper into Brownian motion next week.

To leave you with one final thought: if you had a 1 \mum isolated plastic particle and an aggregate containing many of those 1 \mum particles, which one is more likely to remain suspended in a lake?

The isolated particle! The aggregate has a much larger effective diameter, meaning it will settle much faster and eventually find its way to the sediment. Size dictates the journey.
